children.text: A cluster of a dozen or so islands scattered in the waters off Carles, at the northeastern tip of Panay Island. This hidden hopping destination in West Visayas is known for emerald lagoons between limestone cliffs, white sandbars, and a near-endless feast of scallops.

Islas de Gigantes means "Islands of the Giants" in Spanish. It's a cluster of a dozen or so islands scattered in the Visayan Sea off the municipality of Carles, at the northeastern tip of Panay Island; most residents live on the two largest islands, Gigantes Norte and Gigantes Sur, while the rest are small uninhabited islets and rock formations. The name is said to come from an old legend that oversized coffins and bones, believed to belong to giants, were found in caves on the islands.

The scenery here recalls El Nido or Coron — limestone cliffs and jagged rock formations rising from the sea, white sand beaches hidden among them, sandbars exposed at low tide, and emerald lagoons formed where seawater seeps through cracks in the rock. Yet because it's inconvenient to reach, the islands stayed largely unknown to foreign travelers for a long time, leaving behind a relatively cheap and unpolished atmosphere.

Gigantes is also known as the island of scallops. So many scallops are caught in the surrounding waters that there was once a saying that a single scallop cost only one or two pesos. Even today, hopping tour lunches come piled high with scallops, crab, squid, and shellfish dishes, earning it the nickname "the all-you-can-eat scallop feast."
In

, the massive typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) struck this area and caused heavy damage, but residents rebuilt the community around tourism. Facilities are still basic, so it suits adventurous travelers who enjoy village homestays, beach camping, seafood, and hopping tours more than upscale resorts.

wide. All the islands belong to the municipality of Carles and are divided into four barangays: Asluman and Granada on Gigantes Norte, and Gabi and Lantangan on Gigantes Sur. As of the

census, the population is about 14,300, and the islands are recorded as having more than 70 limestone caves. Carles is a fishing town so rich in marine resources that it's nicknamed "the Alaska of the Philippines." The damage was so severe that there were unofficial reports that more than 90% of the island's houses were destroyed when Haiyan hit on
November 8, 2013
, but today each island has tourist guidance and a tour system in place.
A narrow strip of sand connecting two rocky hills creates Gigantes' iconic scenery. Climb a short rocky path to the viewpoint, and the sea unfolds on both sides in a single sweeping view.

A natural saltwater pool enclosed by limestone cliffs on Gigantes Sur island. Seawater flows in and out through cracks in the rock, giving the water an emerald color, and whether you can enter depends on the tide.
A small stretch of white sand hidden beneath towering rock cliffs, a good spot for swimming and snorkeling during a hopping tour.
A long white sandbar that emerges at low tide, letting you take photos that look like you're walking in the middle of the sea.
A stop for snorkeling in the clear water around this small island, followed by rest on the beach.
Feast on steamed or grilled scallops, crab, squid, and shellfish dishes served as the joiner tour lunch. You can also buy extra scallops at local prices and have them cooked for you.
A lighthouse on a hill along the island's north coast. The old Spanish-era lighthouse was one of 27 lighthouses built before
, but it collapsed in

during Typhoon Fengshen, and today a solar-powered steel tower donated by Japan lights the way. Beside the tower are the ruins of the old keepers' quarters with arched windows still standing, which make a popular photo spot; you can climb up by a short trek or motorcycle taxi and look down over the Visayan Sea and the village.

If the sea is rough and the shared boat doesn't run, you'll have to stay on the island another day, so avoid an itinerary that puts you on a flight to Manila the same day you leave Gigantes. It's safer to book your return flight from Roxas or Iloilo with
a day
to spare.

After the tour ends, return to Bancal Port and board a bus or van to Iloilo
A day tour departing from Iloilo is tight, since the bus travel alone takes
7–8 hours

round trip, and your return can be delayed by sea conditions. If you have time to spare, it's better to stay one night on the island, or fly direct from Manila to Roxas and start from the Carles side.
Cebu Pacific and Philippine Airlines operate daily direct flights from Manila to Roxas Airport (RXS, Capiz Province), taking about
1 hour 15 minutes
. Roxas is closer to Carles than Iloilo is (about
70km
by road), making it the fastest gateway if you're only going to Gigantes, and from Roxas to Carles it takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
by van or bus.
It's about
1 hour 10 minutes
from Manila to Iloilo International Airport (ILO); since there are more flights, most travelers route through Iloilo.
Buses and vans to Carles run from early morning from the Tagbak Terminal (the northbound terminal) in the Jaro district of Iloilo City, taking about
3 hours 30 minutes–4 hours

5–6 hours
via Roxas.
Boats also depart from Estancia Port, so you can choose based on your route.

Bancal Port is the official port of entry and exit for the islands. Places such as Tangke Lagoon can be entered only with the pass you receive after registering at the Bancal tourist information center.
From the Lawaan Terminal in Roxas City, a bus or van to Carles takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
and costs about
per person. From the Carles terminal to Bancal Port is about
30 minutes
by tricycle.
Shared bangkas also leave from Estancia Port once a day around noon. The trip takes about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
and costs about
per person; the schedule changes often, so confirm before departure.
It's about
146km
by road from Iloilo City to Carles. Even if you bring a car, you can't take it onto the islands, so you park it near Bancal Port and board a boat.
Get around the islands on foot or by motorcycle taxi (habal-habal); travel between islands is always by bangka.
Travel agencies in Iloilo and elsewhere run packages of
1 night 2 days to 2 nights 3 days
that bundle transport, accommodation, hopping, and meals, which is more convenient than traveling independently.
From
March
to
May
is the best time, with light winds and calm seas. Clear skies make the lagoon and sandbar water at their most vivid, and the risk of cancelled hopping tours is low.
December–February
is also dry season, but the northeast monsoon (Amihan) can make boat crossings and hopping on the eastern side rough or lead to cancellations on some days.
From
June
to
November
is the rainy and typhoon season, and boats can be grounded for several days at a time due to typhoons, especially
August–November
. During Holy Week, a Philippine public holiday, and early
May
, domestic travelers flock here, filling up accommodation and boats quickly. Tangke Lagoon and the sandbars change dramatically with the tide, so discuss the hopping order with your guide.
Tangke Saltwater Lagoon is closed to tourism for the whole month of
September
, when the southwest monsoon makes the waves rough. Under an executive order from the Carles mayor, entering the lagoon, swimming, and anchoring boats were all banned from
September 1–30, 2026
as well, and it reopened on
October 1
. Since it has closed in the same month every year, if you go then, plan an itinerary without the lagoon and check the latest announcements.

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Most accommodation is in homestays and small resorts in the villages of Gigantes Norte and Gigantes Sur. Fan rooms cost around
a night, while air-conditioned rooms or beach cottages run about

. Beach camping is possible on some islands. Electricity is sometimes limited to certain hours, so check the air conditioning and generator schedule when booking. There are also small accommodations on the Carles mainland near Bancal Port, handy for a late arrival.

Seafood is, without question, the star of the food here. Scallops grilled or steamed with butter and garlic, crab, grilled squid, fish kinilaw, and shellfish soup all appear at tour lunches and at your accommodation. Scallops can be bought cheaply on the spot by weight or count, and many travelers arrange a seafood party through their accommodation. There are no convenience stores on the islands, so buy snacks, drinks, and any food you prefer beforehand in Carles.
For accommodation, Gigantes Hideaway Tourist Inn on Gigantes Norte is consistently featured in many guidebooks, and on the mainland Solina Beach & Nature Resort, about
10–15 minutes

from Bancal Port, is often mentioned. Antonia Beach and Cabugao Gamay Island offer tent stays with almost no electricity, so bring a flashlight and a power bank, and Huni Resort on Sicogon Island in the same municipality of Carles is an alternative if you want a comfortable getaway. Most island restaurants cook to order in a "paruto" style, so let them know one or two hours before mealtime, and tour lunches are often a beachside spread with all-you-can-eat scallops plus fish, chicken, vegetables, and rice.
There are no ATMs on the islands. Since transport, accommodation, tours, and entrance fees must all be paid in cash, withdraw plenty in Iloilo or Roxas beforehand.
Phone signal is unreliable and varies by island and location. Save your accommodation's and tour operator's contact details in advance.
Missing the early morning bus from Iloilo makes it hard to catch the public boat that day. Check the first departure time and leave with plenty of margin.
The rocky paths to the Cabugao Gamay viewpoint and the lighthouse are slippery and sharp. Wear aqua shoes or sandal-style trekking shoes.
There's a lot of spray during bangka rides, so a waterproof pouch or dry bag is essential.
If you're planning to eat a lot of scallops, check for seafood allergies beforehand and bring your own medication.
A
1-night, 2-day
package handles transport connections and the hopping order for you, making it especially convenient for first-time visitors.

On many parts of the island, electricity comes on only for a few hours from dusk into the night and early morning. Bring a fully charged power bank, and Smart tends to have relatively better mobile signal.
Tangke Lagoon closes for the whole of September every year, so if you're going that month, first check with your tour operator whether there's an alternative stop to replace the lagoon.
If you arrive at the Cabugao Gamay Island viewpoint before 9:00 AM, there are fewer people and the light is good. Per-island entrance fees are
per site and are usually included in joiner tours.
On days with high waves, the coast guard can suspend boat service. Don't push for a departure and build a spare day into your schedule.
Tangke Lagoon is enclosed by cliffs and narrow rock gaps, which can be dangerous at high tide or in rough seas. Follow your guide's judgment, and only cliff-dive after confirming the water depth.
Don't touch marine life or coral, or collect shells or coral fragments. Always carry your trash out with you.
Freshness is everything with seafood. Avoid food that's been left out too long, and don't overdo it on raw dishes.
Entrance fees, environmental charges, and boat schedules change often under the Carles municipal government's policies, so check the latest notice.
In
August 2019

, a strong wind warning cut off boat service for about a week, leaving more than 100 tourists stranded on the island. During the southwest monsoon from August to October, coast guard suspensions of boat service can last for days at a time, so arrange travel insurance and plenty of spare days.
Always wear a life jacket while traveling between islands. Small bangkas roll easily in rough water, and the nearest hospital is on the mainland.
